summary: Follow-up on Helix production incident on 2026-03-12 where a high burst of traffic caused sustained KV-cache thrashing and degraded tail latency for a subset of requests. We reviewed root causes, short-term mitigations (cache warming, temporary routing to higher tier capacity), and medium-term reliability improvements (better cache eviction heuristics, capacity reservation, improved observability). Agreed next steps: share logs, run Dedicated benchmarks with Helix workload, and plan a mitigations rollout timeline.
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-15 | 09:00 PDT | 52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Johnson (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (Helix Head of ML), Carlos Rivera (Helix Platform), Priya Nair (Helix SRE), Liam O'Connor (Helix CTO)
---
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we're here to go over the postmortem follow up from Friday's incident, i know it's a lot so we'll try to keep to the key actions -- Diego do you want to start with a quick recap?
[00:18] Diego: yeah sure, so quick recap, on 2026-03-12 at ~14:40 UTC Helix saw a traffic spike from a marketing campaign, the workload had a lot of short prefix patterns which caused the primary KV cache hit rate to drop and the runtime to fall back to more expensive recompute paths. that led to p95/p99 latency spikes and some throttling on our shared hosted pool. we had automated fallback to higher-tier instances but there was also a scheduling backlog that increased tail latencies.
[00:45] Maya: and just to chime in, the spike was way bigger than our normal load and we also had a batch of small requests from internal tooling that stressed the cache in an unexpected way.
[01:02] Carlos: one quick note, some of our internal telemetry uses short TTLs which i think made the cache churn worse, so that's on us too.
[01:15] Diego: absolutely, we saw frequent kv-cache evictions, the prefix cache wasn't matching, and some of the heuristics in the scheduler caused small requests to get pushed to lower-priority queues.
[01:30] Priya: question — when you say fallback to higher tier, was that the Dedicated pool or an internal burst lane on hosted?
[01:37] Avery: good question — it was the higher tier hosted pool (we route based on capacity tiers), we didn't failover to Helix's Dedicated instance because that wasn't provisioned.
[01:47] Liam: quick clarity — is Dedicated something we can spin up quickly, like reserve for a week if we need?
[01:54] Diego: we can provision Dedicated capacity but usually need a short provisioning window; for emergencies we can do temporary reserved capacity if agreeable. there was a note about cost tradeoffs — we can cover that after.
[02:12] Avery: okay, let's run through root cause categories: 1) workload shape (many short prefixes), 2) cache tuning and TTLs, 3) scheduler/backpressure handling under burst, 4) lack of reserved capacity for critical routes.
[02:30] [..fast-forward.. some discussion on specific logs..]
[07:12] Diego: from the logs we captured, there's a period where per-shard KV miss rate climbs from ~8% to >40% over ~3 minutes, and then the runtime started doing more recompute leading to 4-6x token generation CPU. the autoscaler didn't react quickly because the scheduler queue depth masked the need, so we had to manually bump routes.
[07:38] Maya: is the 40% number accurate? we saw different numbers in our telemetry — maybe our instrumentation is counting different key shapes.
[07:46] Diego: right, some prop names got normalized differently in our exporter — so the absolute numbers vary but trend matches.
[08:00] Carlos: okay makes sense, so root causes sound plausible. what are the recommended mitigations?
[08:08] Diego: short term: enable prefix warming for the busiest routes, increase cache size for Helix routes, temporarily cap small-request concurrency to avoid hammering, and route critical traffic to reserved high-tier capacity during large campaigns.
[08:25] Avery: medium term: revise eviction heuristics to prefer keeping hot prefixes across shards, add an adaptive TTL policy based on observed reuse, and improve autoscaler signals to include queue-depth and cache-miss-rate.
[08:40] Priya: will that require changes on our side? like instrumenting different metrics?
[08:45] Diego: we'll need Helix to share anonymized prompt shapes and traffic windows, and if you can label critical routes that helps with routing and reserved capacity policies.
[09:00] Maya: we can provide that, we'll scrub any PII.
[09:06] Lina: action — Redwood to share KV-cache and scheduler logs we captured.
[09:12] Diego: yes i already pulled the debug logs; i'll package them and share the S3 link. some logs have noisy hostnames — expect a bit of messy fields, transcription there may be mismatches.
[09:24] [15:00] discussion about mitigation timeline and ramping Dedicated capacity
[15:33] Liam: high level question — how do we avoid this from happening again during seasonal spikes, we can't afford repeated degradation.
[15:40] Avery: we propose a three-pronged plan: 1) short-term operational guardrails (cache warming, routing to reserved for known campaigns), 2) probabilistic caching improvements in the runtime, and 3) capacity reservations for peak windows.
[15:58] Carlos: what's the typical lead time and cost for those reservations?
[16:04] Diego: provisioning Dedicated typically takes 2-5 business days for capacity matching; cost depends on size but we can run a pilot on a smaller Dedicated pool for the worst routes to prove ROI.
[16:18] Maya: could we do a synthetic benchmark to validate before committing?
[16:22] Diego: absolutely — we'll run the Helix prompt set against a Dedicated instance and provide latency/cost breakdowns.
[16:30] Avery: ok, we'll also share a recommended config (batching, quant profile, cache size) for the pilot.
[17:02] [22:15] Priya: on alerting, during the incident our SLO playbook triggered but the on-call didn't immediately see cache-miss signal. can we add a sentinel alert?
[22:28] Diego: yes, that's on our list — add cache-miss-rate and queue-depth composite alert to the Helix route. Lina will coordinate.
[22:40] Lina: i'll add it to the action items and coordinate runbook updates.
[22:50] Maya: about security/compliance — we need to confirm log retention, PII scrubbing, and KMS usage for any logs shared.
[23:00] Avery: Redwood will send SOC2 report and KMS/encryption docs, we'll redact sensitive fields in logs and provide guidance on safe sharing.
[23:12] Diego: note, some of our internal debug traces contain internal hostnames — we'll scrub those before upload.
[23:20] [28:00] brief cross-talk, minor audio issues, some words merged "KV" becomes "K V" in auto transcript
[28:50] Carlos: one more technical ask, can the runtime keep hot prefixes across restarts? we had a few workers recycle and lost cache state which worsened the hit-rate.
[29:02] Diego: we're exploring persistent cache snapshots and faster warmup; not trivial but feasible. medium term effort.
[29:18] Maya: would that require on-prem changes? we run hybrid: some traffic through our VPC peering and some through hosted.
[29:26] Diego: the hybrid routing should be fine; snapshots would live in a shared cache store which we can host in VPC for Private deployments. for hosted we'd use encrypted internal storage.
[29:40] Priya: okay good.
[31:00] [35:00] Discussion on cost vs. reliability tradeoffs, mention of comparing to Anthropic and Bedrock for reserved capacity economics
[35:28] Avery: summary, agreed next steps: Redwood shares logs and SOC2, Helix shares traffic profile and prompt set, Redwood runs Dedicated benchmark with Helix dataset, coordinate alerting/runbook updates, and meet next week to review results.
[36:02] Lina: proposed follow-up meeting Thursday 2026-03-18 10am PT; does that work?
[36:10] Maya: yes works for me.
[36:12] Liam: ok confirmed.
[36:20] [41:00] quick Q&A on instrumentation mismatches and how export normalization affects cache metrics
[41:35] Diego: we'll include a mapping doc that explains how Redwood aggregates keys and normalizes prefixes so you can reconcile numbers.
[41:50] Maya: perfect that's helpful.
[42:10] Avery: anything else? if not we'll wrap \u2014 thanks everybody for the constructive session.
[42:22] Carlos: thanks.
[42:25] Priya: thanks, appreciate the quick turnaround.
[42:30] [End]

Meeting recap (short): Helix production incident due to burst workload and KV-cache thrashing. Short-term mitigations: cache warming, route to reserved capacity, cap small-request concurrency. Medium-term: adaptive TTLs, eviction heuristic changes, persistent cache snapshots, improve autoscaler signals. Action items and owners recorded. Next meeting 2026-03-18 10:00 PT.
